item.title: High-entropy molecular contacts enable high-efficiency and stable perovskite solar cells
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02028-5 High-entropy molecular contacts made by blending self-assembled molecules improve hole transport through diverse packing modes. Solar cells incorporating these contacts achieve a certified power conversion efficiency of 27.31% and negligible loss after 1,300 h of operation at 85 °C.

item.title: Nonlinear circular dichroism reveals the local Berry curvature
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02025-8 The nonlinear high harmonic circular dichroism for crystals with broken time-reversal symmetry is found to be directly proportional to the local Berry curvature, and it can be directly probed via ultrafast all-optical measurements.

item.title: Intermolecular decoupling of C<sub>60</sub> suppresses interfacial recombination in perovskite solar cells
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02030-x Interfacial recombination in perovskite solar cells is mitigated through a vapour-phase molecular passivation method using trialkylamines, disrupting C60 packing. This approach results in a power conversion efficiency of up to 27.2% while maintaining stability.

item.title: Solid-state emissive acceptors enable thermally accessible radiative pathways for efficient organic solar cells
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02009-8 Solid-state emissive guest acceptors enhance organic solar cells by establishing thermally accessible radiative pathways, significantly reducing non-radiative voltage loss end enabling ternary blend devices with a certified power conversion efficiency of 20.84%.

item.title: New high-frequency method boosts 2D material readout for next-gen quantum computers
item.description: Quantum computers represent a next step in the fast-paced evolution of technology. Using quantum bits (qubits), they have the potential to run certain calculations exponentially faster than conventional computers. However, developing and fine-tuning quantum computers requires an enormous number of repetitive tests. To accelerate quantum technology development, we need a method that can read quantum states at ultrafast speeds.

item.title: A highway instead of a racetrack: Strong coupling of light and sound in an optical fiber
item.description: For the first time, scientists have achieved strong coupling between light and long-lived acoustic vibrations in an optical fiber. Optical fibers are used in both classical telecommunications and quantum communication and could serve not only as connections between computing nodes but also as quantum processors themselves in the future. The results, published in Nature Physics, pave the way for new technologies in quantum signal processing.

item.title: Even or odd numbers: A single molecule makes all the difference in the quantum world
item.description: The researchers in the Quantum Detection Microscopy group at CIC nanoGUNE, in collaboration with chemists at CiQUS of the University of Santiago de Compostela, have demonstrated that adding or removing a single molecule from a quantum chain can fundamentally change its interaction with a superconductor.

Laser pulses bring order to a quantum material's tiny electrical regions
item.description: Physicists at Auburn University have used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged "islands" inside a crystal. The discovery helps answer a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows how light could be used to control its behavior—a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information.
